newsitem.title: USA: Tight supplies, brisk exports boost CBOT rice.
newsitem.headline: Tight supplies, brisk exports boost CBOT rice.

text.p: A combination of tight supplies and prospects of good exports drove rice futures on the Chicago Board of Trade to end sharply higher in volatile trading, analysts and traders said.
Rice closed higher with March at $12.155 per cwt, up 29 cents.
"Long grain stocks are very tight in the U.S.," said Gail Cramer, professor of agricultural economics at the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reduced 1996/97 (August/July) U.S. rice ending stocks to 24.3 million cwt from 25.3 million in January.
The long grain portion of that carryover was down one million cwt to 9.3 million cwt and it was that inventory that was still in debate and questioned, analysts said.

"There is still a bullish scenario which suggests the USDA agricultural production numbers as well as the acreage numbers are still overstated," said Neauman Coleman, senior vice president, futures at Dean Witter.
"This is a supply-driven market," he added.
The USDA raised its export estimate to 75.0 million cwt from 74.0 million a month ago.

"In addition to the increase in exports, there are number of individuals that think the USDA has overestimated long grain production, which would further lower carryover stocks and put additional upward pressure on long grain rice prices," Cramer said.
USDA pegged 1996/97 long grain rice production at 113.5 million cwt, unchanged from January but down from 121.7 million in 1995/96.
Another factor was that exports of rough rice have the been the driving element of the long grain prices this year, Coleman said.

U.S. rough rice exports in the first half of the 1996/97 (August-July) marketing year totaled 270,400 tonnes, up 73 percent from the 156,300 tonnes exported in the same period last year, the USDA said in a report for the week ended January 30.
Cramer joined the bullish chorus by pointing out that Colombia was in the market for additional long grain rice.
"Of course, we are aware of North Korea's needs for additional rice which would indirectly influence the market," Cramer added.

One U.S. rice exporter also noted a lot of business from the West Coast to Japan of medium grain rice and a great deal of U.S. paddy rice moving into Central and South America. "That has given our market a boost," he said.
Even the technical picture appeared to be positive. From October 1996 to January 31, 1997, CBOT March rice rose 24.5 percent to $12.45, said Hans Kashyap, president of Analytics Research Corp.

"The market is recovering from a reaction off of that high," Kashyap said. "It fell 7.5 percent to $11.50 basis March into the first week of February 1997 and is now resuming its upward trend. You have to be bullish on this market," Kashyap said.
